_meta.descricao: Saints whose doctrine the Church recognizes as an eminent reference for all of Christendom.
_meta.aviso: Brings together the 37 Doctors of the Church recognized to date. For editorial use, always consult the official documents of proclamation.
_meta.revisao_editorial: The field 'ano_proclamacao' records the year of the pontifical act proclaiming the saint a Doctor of the Church. Honorific titles are those consecrated by tradition and by the magisterium, not formulations of this collection.
fontes_gerais: Pontifical acts of proclamation of Doctors of the Church (vatican.va)

itens.resumo: Bishop of Hippo (354-430), one of the first four Doctors of the Latin Church; author of the «Confessions» and «The City of God», he received from tradition the title «Doctor of Grace».
itens.corpo:
Aurelius Augustine was born in Tagaste, in Roman North Africa (today Souk Ahras, in Algeria), on November 13, 354, the son of Patricius, a pagan, and of Saint Monica, whose prayers marked his life. He passed through Carthage, was a professor of rhetoric in Milan (384) and, before his conversion, adhered to Manichaeism and then to Neoplatonism. In August 386, in a garden in Milan, he heard a child's refrain, «tolle lege» («take and read»); opening the Letter to the Romans (13:13-14), he was converted. He was baptized by Saint Ambrose at the Easter Vigil of 387. Ordained a priest in 391, he was made Bishop of Hippo Regius in 395, and governed that see for about thirty-five years.

Two great controversies consumed much of his energy. The Donatist controversy, born of divisions that arose during the persecutions, was debated and condemned at the Council of Carthage in 411: against the thesis that the validity of baptism depended on the worthiness of the minister, Augustine affirmed that it is Christ who administers the sacrament, and that the Church, in this world, contains wheat and weeds. The Pelagian controversy, concerning grace and original sin, saw him set his doctrine of the absolute necessity of divine grace against the synergist position — which earned him the title «Doctor Gratiae».

His work is immense. The «Confessions», written between 397 and 400, are an autobiographical narrative in the form of a prayer to God — the first nine books are autobiographical and the last four are philosophical in character, on memory, time and creation. «The City of God», composed between 413 and 426, was occasioned by the sack of Rome by the Visigoths of Alaric in 410, which led the pagans to blame the Christians for the fall of the City; in twenty-two books, it contrasts the «earthly city», founded on love of self, with the «city of God», founded on love of God, and sketches a Christian philosophy of history. He also wrote treatises on the Trinity, on grace and on the interpretation of Scripture, as well as hundreds of sermons and letters.

He died in Hippo on August 28, 430. He was canonized by popular acclamation and, in 1298, Pope Boniface VIII — in a decree that ordered the celebration of his feasts — recognized him as a Doctor of the Church among the first four: Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory the Great and himself. He is counted among the four great Latin Doctors; in the Orthodox Church, although he is revered as a saint, some of his doctrines are not accepted. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on August 28.
fontes: Saint Augustine, «Confessions» (Books I-XIII, written between 397 and 400)
Pope Boniface VIII, decree proclaiming the first four Doctors of the Latin Church (1298)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 27 (quotation from the «Confessions», I, 1, 1)

itens.resumo: Thirteenth-century Dominican friar, author of the «Summa Theologiae»; proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius V in 1567 and called the Angelic Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Thomas was born in Roccasecca, in the Kingdom of Naples, around 1225, into a noble family. Against the wishes of his relatives — who kept him in captivity for almost a year to dissuade him — he entered the Order of Preachers (Dominicans) around 1244. He studied in Paris and in Cologne under Saint Albert the Great and taught in Paris, Rome and Naples, during one of the most turbulent periods of the Parisian university debate: he fought the Latin Averroism of Siger of Brabant and the thesis of the «double truth», above all in the «De unitate intellectus contra Averroistas» (1270), defending the harmony between faith and reason and the immortality of the individual soul.

His principal work is the «Summa Theologiae», an ordered exposition of Christian doctrine in three parts (plus a Supplement added by disciples), divided into 614 questions and about 3,125 articles, which articulates faith with philosophy, especially with Aristotle, whom he calls «the Philosopher». The work was left unfinished in the part on the sacraments. He also wrote the «Summa contra Gentiles» (four books, 1259-1265), commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle, as well as an extensive body of work connected with the liturgy.

Tradition attributes to him the liturgical texts of the solemnity of Corpus Christi, instituted by the bull «Transiturus hoc mundo» of Pope Urban IV (1264): the hymns «Pange lingua» (with the stanza «Tantum ergo»), «Lauda Sion» (the sequence of the Mass), «Verbum supernum prodiens» (with the «O salutaris hostia») and the «Adoro te devote». As for the latter, however, its authorship is disputed: twentieth-century scholars, such as Eschmann, observed that no manuscript from the first fifty years after Thomas's death attributes it to him, although tradition considers him its author — the question remains open.

He died on the way to the Council of Lyon, at the abbey of Fossanova, on March 7, 1274. He was canonized in 1323 by John XXII. On April 11, 1567, Pope Saint Pius V, in the wake of the Council of Trent, proclaimed him a Doctor of the Church by the bull «Mirabilis Deus» and made his feast equal to that of the great Latin Fathers — which earned him the title «Angelic Doctor» (Doctor Angelicus). Leo XIII, in the encyclical «Aeterni Patris» (1879), recommended his study in Catholic schools and declared him the «Common Doctor» of the Church; the Second Vatican Council mentions him as a master in theological formation. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on January 28.
fontes: Saint Thomas Aquinas, «Summa Theologiae» (three parts, c. 614 questions)
Pope Pius V, bull «Mirabilis Deus» (April 11, 1567), proclamation of Thomas as a Doctor of the Church
Pope Urban IV, bull «Transiturus hoc mundo» (1264), institution of the solemnity of Corpus Christi
Second Vatican Council, Decree «Optatam Totius» (1965), no. 16

itens.titulo: Saint Teresa of Ávila, Doctor of the Church
itens.resumo: Reformer of the Carmelite Order and teacher of prayer; on September 27, 1970, she became the first woman proclaimed a Doctor of the Church, after centuries of refusal marked by the argument of «obstat sexus».
itens.corpo:
Teresa of Jesus (Ávila, March 28, 1515 – Alba de Tormes, October 4, 1582), a Carmelite of Ávila, undertook the reform of the Carmelite Order beginning at the Convent of the Incarnation, where observance of the rule had grown lax. On August 24, 1562, she founded the first convent reformed according to the primitive rule, that of Saint Joseph of Ávila, known as the «Convent of las Madres», with a number of nuns initially set by her at thirteen. In 1567 she met Saint John of the Cross, and together they extended the reform to the friars; from then on, over some twenty years, she established seventeen convents, all founded personally by her except one, stretching from Medina del Campo (1567) and Valladolid (1568) to Seville, Burgos and Granada (1582).

Her written work was born of this life of foundations and of intense prayer. The «Book of Her Life» (autobiography), the «Way of Perfection», the «Interior Castle» (or «Mansions», a masterpiece written in 1577) and the «Book of Foundations» describe the path of prayer from the first steps to union with God, with constant insistence on humility, truth and fraternal life. Her mystical doctrine was an object of suspicion: for a period she was under investigation by the Spanish Inquisition, and her manner of silent prayer was seen by some as less devout than vocal prayer; the reformed order itself was only officially recognized by the Holy See in 1578, and declared separate from the old trunk in 1594, twelve years after her death.

Five years before her canonization, in 1617, the Cortes Generales proclaimed her patroness of Spain, and the University of Salamanca conferred on her the diploma of «Doctor ecclesiae», an academic title distinct from the papal honor. She was beatified on April 24, 1614, by Paul V and canonized on March 12, 1622, by Gregory XV.

Recognition as a Doctor of the Church was long and controversial. In 1923, Pius XI rejected the request with the pithy formula, attributed to the rapporteur Monsignor Aurelio Galli: «obstat sexus» (her sex prevents it). It was Paul VI who took up the cause on his own initiative and, in the Vatican Basilica, on September 27, 1970, proclaimed her a Doctor by the Apostolic Letter «Multiformis sapientia Dei», which greets her as «Teresa of Jesus, great and noble», and recognizes her with the title «Mater Spiritualium» (Mother of Spirituality). A few days later the same Pontiff proclaimed Saint Catherine of Siena a Doctor; the two were thus the first women to receive the title in the history of the Church. Her liturgical memorial is celebrated on October 15.
fontes: Paul VI, Apostolic Letter «Multiformis sapientia Dei» (September 27, 1970)
Saint Teresa of Jesus, «Interior Castle (Mansions)», «Book of Her Life», «Way of Perfection» and «Book of Foundations»
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 2709 (quoting the «Book of Her Life», 8, 5)
Congregation for Divine Worship, «Positio» on the doctorate of Saint Teresa of Jesus (1970)
Federation of the Discalced Carmelite Sisters, historical aid on the proclamation of September 27, 1970

itens.resumo: Bishop of Milan in the fourth century, one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church; he baptized Saint Augustine and is the author of moral treatises and liturgical hymns.
itens.corpo:
Ambrose was born around 339 in Augusta Treverorum (present-day Trier), the son of a high official of the Roman Empire. He was trained in rhetoric and law and was serving as governor of the province of Liguria and Emilia, based in Milan, when, in 374, he was acclaimed bishop of the city by the people, while still a catechumen — he received baptism, the other orders of the priesthood and episcopal ordination in rapid succession.

As bishop, he stood out for his preaching and for his firmness before political power, to the point of imposing public penance on Emperor Theodosius after the massacre of Thessalonica. His preaching on Scripture played a decisive role in the conversion of Augustine of Hippo, whom he baptized at Easter in 387. Among his works, the «De officiis ministrorum», a treatise on morals for the clergy, the «De fide», on the divinity of Christ, and hymns that became a model of Latin hymnody, such as the «Veni redemptor gentium», stand out.

He died in Milan in 397. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Latin Church by Boniface VIII in 1298, together with Jerome, Augustine and Gregory the Great — the first four to receive the title. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on December 7, the date of his episcopal ordination.
fontes: Saint Augustine, «Confessions», Book VI (on the influence of Ambrose)

itens.resumo: Monk and priest of the 4th-5th centuries, translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate); one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church.
itens.corpo:
Eusebius Jerome was born around 347 in Stridon, on the border between Dalmatia and Pannonia. He studied rhetoric in Rome, traveled through the East, lived as a hermit in the desert of Chalcis, and was ordained a priest in Antioch. He served as secretary to Pope Damasus I in Rome before settling permanently in Bethlehem, where he founded a monastery.

His central work is the Vulgate, a translation of the Bible into Latin from the original Hebrew and Greek texts, undertaken at the request of Pope Damasus and completed over the course of decades; it became the standard biblical text of the Latin Church for more than a thousand years, and its authority was confirmed by the Council of Trent. He also wrote biblical commentaries and the «De viris illustribus» (a catalogue of Christian writers), and left a vast correspondence marked by erudition and a polemical temperament.

He died in Bethlehem in 420. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Latin Church by Boniface VIII in 1298, alongside Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory the Great. He is considered the patron saint of translators, librarians, and scholars of Scripture; his liturgical memorial is celebrated on September 30.
fontes: Council of Trent, Session IV (1546), on the authority of the Vulgate

itens.resumo: Pope from 590 to 604, author of the «Pastoral Rule» and the «Dialogues»; one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church.
itens.corpo:
Gregory was born around 540 in Rome, into a senatorial family. He held the office of prefect of the city before renouncing public life to become a Benedictine monk; he founded six monasteries and transformed his own family home, on the Caelian Hill, into a monastery under the rule of Saint Benedict. He was sent as papal legate to Constantinople and, in 590, was elected Bishop of Rome against his will.

As pope, he reorganized the administration of Church properties, aided the people of Rome during famines and invasions, and sent the monk Augustine of Canterbury to evangelize the Anglo-Saxons. He wrote the «Regula Pastoralis» (Pastoral Rule), on the duties of the bishop, a work that became a reference for ecclesiastical governance throughout the Middle Ages; the «Dialogues», accounts of the lives and miracles of Italian saints, among them Saint Benedict; and numerous homilies on the Gospels and on the Book of Job (the «Moralia in Job»). Later tradition attributes to him the reform of Roman liturgical chant, which came to be called Gregorian chant.

He died in Rome in 604. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Latin Church by Boniface VIII in 1298, together with Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine. He is, together with Leo the Great and Nicholas I, one of the few popes to whom tradition attributes the title "the Great." His liturgical memorial is celebrated on September 3.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Alexandria in the fourth century, the foremost defender of the Nicene faith against Arianism; one of the four great Doctors of the Greek Church.
itens.corpo:
Athanasius was born around 296-298, in Alexandria or its vicinity. While still a deacon, he accompanied Bishop Alexander of Alexandria to the Council of Nicaea (325), where he distinguished himself in defending the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father against the doctrine of Arius. He succeeded Alexander as Bishop of Alexandria in 328.

His episcopate, which lasted more than four decades, was marked by five exiles imposed by emperors favorable to Arianism — a period during which he continued to write and to defend the Nicene faith throughout Christendom. Among his works, the «Against the Pagans» and the «On the Incarnation of the Word» stand out, a classic exposition of the doctrine of the redemptive incarnation, as well as the «Orations against the Arians» and the «Life of Antony», a biography of the Egyptian monk that spread the ideal of monasticism in the West.

He died in Alexandria in 373. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Greek Church by Pius V in 1568, together with Basil the Great, Gregory Nazianzen, and John Chrysostom. Tradition remembers him as a "pillar of the Church," for the firmness with which he defended Trinitarian orthodoxy in one of the gravest moments of doctrinal crisis in Christian history.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the 4th century, lawgiver of Eastern monasticism, and one of the three great hierarchs of the Greek Church.
itens.corpo:
Basil was born around 330 in Caesarea in Cappadocia, into a family of saints — among his siblings were Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina the Younger. He studied rhetoric and philosophy in Athens, where he formed a friendship with Gregory of Nazianzus, and after a journey through the monasteries of Egypt and Syria he devoted himself to monastic life in Cappadocia. He was ordained bishop of Caesarea in 370.

He is considered the father of Eastern monasticism: his Rules — the "Longer Rule" and the "Shorter Rule" — organized the community life of monks and remain normative for Byzantine monasticism to this day. He also wrote the treatise «On the Holy Spirit», in defense of the divinity of the third Person of the Trinity, the «Hexaemeron», homilies on the six days of creation, and contributed to the composition of the liturgy that bears his name, still used in the Churches of the Byzantine rite on solemn occasions.

He died in Caesarea in 379. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Greek Church by Pius V in 1568, together with Gregory of Nazianzus, Athanasius, and John Chrysostom. With the latter and Gregory of Nazianzus, he is venerated in the East as one of the "Three Holy Hierarchs".
fontes: Saint Basil the Great, «De Spiritu Sancto»

itens.resumo: Cappadocian bishop and theologian of the fourth century, called "the Theologian" for the depth of his Trinitarian doctrine.
itens.corpo:
Gregory was born around 329 near Nazianzus, in Cappadocia, the son of the local bishop, who was also named Gregory. He studied in Caesarea, Alexandria and Athens, where he met Basil the Great, with whom he maintained a friendship and collaboration throughout his life. He was ordained a priest against his will by his own father and, later, a bishop, briefly holding the see of Constantinople during the Council of 381.

He is remembered above all for the "Theological Orations", five sermons delivered in Constantinople that set forth, with rigor and literary beauty, the doctrine of the Trinity and of the divinity of the Holy Spirit, decisive for the definitive formulation of the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. He also left poems, among them a long autobiographical poem, and numerous letters.

He died around 390. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Greek Church by Pius V in 1568, together with Basil the Great, Athanasius and John Chrysostom. He is one of the only men in the Christian tradition to whom the title "the Theologian" is attributed, alongside the Apostle John and Symeon the New Theologian.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Constantinople in the 4th-5th centuries, a celebrated preacher whose nickname, "Golden Mouth," became his very name.
itens.corpo:
John was born around 347 in Antioch of Syria. He was trained in rhetoric under the pagan Libanius, lived as an ascetic, and was ordained a presbyter in Antioch in 386, where he became renowned as a preacher — hundreds of his homilies on almost all the books of Scripture survive. In 397 he was elected, against his will, Patriarch of Constantinople.

As bishop of the imperial capital, he undertook reforms of the clergy and of life at court that earned him powerful enemies, among them the Empress Eudoxia; he was deposed by a rigged synod and exiled twice, dying on the way to his second exile. His homilies — on Genesis, the Psalms, the Gospels of Matthew and John, and the Letters of Paul — form one of the largest bodies of patristic preaching that have come down to us, marked by a literal interpretation of Scripture and a strong moral appeal, above all on behalf of the poor.

He died in 407, in Comana in Pontus. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Greek Church by Pius V in 1568, alongside Basil the Great, Gregory Nazianzen, and Athanasius. He is one of the "Three Holy Hierarchs" of the East and the patron saint of preachers.
fontes: Saint John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew
Saint John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of John

itens.resumo: Franciscan friar and theologian of the 13th century, seventh Minister General of the Order; called the Seraphic Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Giovanni di Fidanza was born in 1221 in Bagnoregio, in Lazio. He entered the Order of Friars Minor around 1243 and studied in Paris, where he received the religious name Bonaventure and became a master of theology alongside Thomas Aquinas, with whom he maintained a friendship and intellectual dialogue. In 1257 he was elected Minister General of the Franciscans, an office he held for seventeen years, giving the Order, then internally divided, juridical and spiritual stability.

His work combines scholastic rigor and Franciscan mysticism. The «Itinerarium mentis in Deum» ("The Soul's Journey into God") describes the soul's ascent to God through the contemplation of creation, of itself, and finally of God in himself; he also wrote commentaries on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, the «Legenda Maior», the official biography of Saint Francis of Assisi, and spiritual treatises such as the «Lignum Vitae».

He died in Lyon in 1274, during the Second Council of Lyon, in which he was participating as a cardinal-bishop. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Sixtus V in 1588, with the title of Seraphic Doctor, in reference to Franciscan spirituality. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on July 15.

itens.resumo: Benedictine monk and Archbishop of Canterbury, considered the father of medieval Scholasticism; author of the ontological argument for the existence of God.
itens.corpo:
Anselm was born around 1033 in Aosta, then part of the Kingdom of Burgundy. After years of wandering, he entered the Benedictine abbey of Bec, in Normandy, where he was a disciple and successor of Lanfranc as prior and later abbot. In 1093 he was appointed Archbishop of Canterbury, against his will, an office in which he confronted two English kings, William II and Henry I, in defense of the freedom of the Church, suffering two exiles.

He is the author of the «Monologion» and the «Proslogion», in the latter of which he formulated the famous ontological argument: the existence of God would follow from the very idea of a being "than which nothing greater can be conceived." In the «Cur Deus Homo» ("Why God Became Man"), he sets forth one of the first systematic theories of the vicarious satisfaction of Christ for the redemption of mankind. His method, summed up in the formula "faith seeking understanding" (fides quaerens intellectum), marked the birth of Scholastic theology.

He died in Canterbury in 1109. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Clement XI in 1720. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on April 21.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Seville in the 6th-7th centuries, author of the "Etymologies," an encyclopedia that preserved the learning of antiquity for the Middle Ages.
itens.corpo:
Isidore was born around 560, probably in Cartagena, in Visigothic Hispania, into a family that produced three other saints: his brothers Leander and Fulgentius, and his sister Florentina. He succeeded Leander as bishop of Seville around 600 and presided over councils important for the organization of the Church in Visigothic Spain, among them the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), which ordered the creation of cathedral schools in every diocese.

His most influential work is the "Etymologies" (or "Origines"), a vast compilation in twenty books that gathers and organizes Greco-Roman knowledge in grammar, rhetoric, medicine, law, natural history, and theology, and which served as a reference work throughout medieval Europe until the Renaissance. He also wrote the "Chronica Maiora" (Universal Chronicle), the "De viris illustribus," and treatises on nature and on the Christian faith.

He died in Seville in 636. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Innocent XIII in 1722. Because of his role in preserving and transmitting ancient learning, historians consider him one of the last scholars of the ancient world; in recent times, he is also informally venerated as the patron saint of the internet and of computer users, by analogy with his encyclopedic work.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Ravenna in the 5th century, famous for his brief and dense homilies; called the Doctor of Homilies.
itens.corpo:
Peter was born around 380 in Imola, in the region of Emilia. He was ordained bishop of Ravenna, then the imperial seat of the West, around 433, with the support, according to tradition, of Emperor Valentinian III and his mother, Galla Placidia.

About 176 of his sermons remain, preserved by Archbishop Felix of Ravenna in the 8th century. They are characterized by brevity and conciseness — Peter himself justified not going on at length so as not to weary his listeners — but also by theological density, dealing with the Creed and the Incarnation, and refuting heresies such as Arianism and Eutychian Monophysitism; he also wrote a letter to Eutyches condemning his Christological doctrine, which played a role in the preparation of the Council of Chalcedon (451).

He died around 450, in Imola, to which he had returned. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XIII in 1729, with the title Doctor of Homilies — his very surname, "Chrysologus," already means "golden word" in Greek. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on July 30.

itens.resumo: Monk, cardinal and ecclesiastical reformer of the eleventh century, one of the chief promoters of the reform of the Church that preceded Gregory VII.
itens.corpo:
Peter was born around 1007 in Ravenna, orphaned early and raised in difficult conditions by an older brother. He studied in Faenza and Parma and distinguished himself as a teacher before embracing monastic life at the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, of Benedictine eremitical observance, of which he became prior and which he reformed and expanded with new foundations.

He was one of the great promoters of the reform of the Church in the eleventh century: he vehemently fought simony (the sale of ecclesiastical offices) and the concubinage of the clergy, above all in the «Liber Gomorrhianus», and wrote numerous treatises and letters on ecclesiastical discipline and spiritual life, among them the «De Divina Omnipotentia». He was created Cardinal Bishop of Ostia in 1057 and was employed by the popes in delicate legations, including the reconciliation of Milan with Rome.

He died in Faenza in 1072, while returning from a papal mission to Ravenna. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Leo XII in 1828. Benedict XVI described him, in a catechesis on the Fathers and Doctors of the Church, as a man "a lover of solitude and, at the same time, fearless, personally committed to the task of reform".
fontes: Benedict XVI, General Audience on Saint Peter Damian (2009)

itens.resumo: Twelfth-century Cistercian abbot, preacher of the Second Crusade and master of mystical theology; called the Mellifluous Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Bernard was born around 1090 in Fontaine-lès-Dijon, in Burgundy, to a noble family. In 1112 he entered the newly founded Cistercian monastery of Cîteaux, bringing with him about thirty relatives and friends, and in 1115 he was sent to found the abbey of Clairvaux, which he governed as abbot until his death, while the Cistercian Order was expanding throughout Europe through foundations linked, in large part, to his personal influence.

His work combines theology, mysticism and ecclesial action: the "Sermons on the Song of Songs," unfinished, set forth the union of the soul with God in the language of spousal love; the "De consideratione," addressed to Pope Eugene III, deals with spiritual governance; the "De diligendo Deo" describes the degrees of the love of God. Bernard intervened actively in the life of the Church of his time: he supported Pope Innocent II against an antipope, opposed the theological rationalism of Abelard, and, at the request of Eugene III, preached the Second Crusade (1146).

He died at Clairvaux in 1153. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius VIII in 1830, with the title of Mellifluous Doctor ("of sweet eloquence"), for the quality of his prose and his preaching. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on August 20.
fontes: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermons on the Song of Songs
Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, "De diligendo Deo"

itens.resumo: Bishop of Poitiers in the fourth century, the chief defender of the Nicene faith in the West against Arianism; called the "Hammer of the Arians."
itens.corpo:
Hilary was born around 310 in Poitiers, in Gaul, to a pagan family, and converted to Christianity as an adult through reading Scripture, before being elected bishop of his native city around 350.

He devoted a large part of his episcopate to combating Arianism, then dominant among the political and ecclesiastical elites of the Empire, which cost him exile in Phrygia (356-360), decreed by the Emperor Constantius II. During his exile, he came into contact with Eastern theology and wrote his greatest work, the «De Trinitate», in twelve books, a systematic exposition of Trinitarian faith that became a reference for later Latin theology; he also wrote the «De synodis», on the formulas of faith of the Eastern synods, and biblical commentaries.

He died around 367, in Poitiers. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius IX in 1851. Tradition has given him the titles "Hammer of the Arians" (Malleus Arianorum) and "Athanasius of the West," because of the similarity between his struggle against Arianism and that of the bishop of Alexandria in the East.

itens.resumo: Neapolitan bishop of the eighteenth century, founder of the Redemptorists and author of the «Moral Theology»; patron of confessors and moralists.
itens.corpo:
Alphonsus was born in 1696 in Marianella, near Naples, into a noble family; he studied law and practiced as a brilliant lawyer before, at the age of 27, abandoning his legal career to be ordained a priest. He devoted himself to popular evangelization, especially among the peasants of the rural areas near Naples, and in 1732 he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer (Redemptorists), dedicated to preaching popular missions.

His most influential work is the «Theologia Moralis», a treatise that sought a balanced path between Jansenist rigorism and laxism, giving rise to what is called "equiprobabilism"; it went through dozens of editions and shaped the formation of confessors for generations. He also wrote widely circulated works of popular spirituality, such as «The Glories of Mary» and «Visits to the Most Blessed Sacrament», as well as hymns and devotional texts in Neapolitan. He was appointed bishop of Sant'Agata dei Goti in 1762.

He died in Pagani, near Naples, in 1787. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius IX in 1871, with the title Most Zealous Doctor. Pius XII declared him patron of confessors and moralists in 1950.
fontes: Saint Alphonsus Liguori, «The Glories of Mary»
Pius XII, act of proclamation as patron of confessors and moralists (April 26, 1950)

itens.resumo: Bishop of Geneva in the 16th-17th centuries, master of spirituality for the laity and co-founder of the Order of the Visitation; called the Doctor of Charity.
itens.corpo:
Francis was born in 1567 in the castle of Sales, in Savoy. He studied law and theology in Paris and Padua and, against the wishes of his father, who wanted him to be a magistrate, he was ordained a priest and devoted himself to the mission of winning back to Catholicism the region of the Chablais, which was largely Calvinist, through preaching and writings of great persuasiveness and gentleness. He was appointed Bishop of Geneva in 1602, although, because of the Protestant rule in the city, he resided in Annecy.

He is the author of the "Introduction to the Devout Life," a guide to spirituality written for the laity which shows that it is possible to seek holiness amid the occupations of the world, and of the "Treatise on the Love of God," a more systematic exposition of his spiritual doctrine, centered on trust and loving abandonment to the divine will. With Saint Jane de Chantal, he founded the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary in 1610.

He died in Lyon in 1622. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius IX in 1877, with the title of Doctor of Charity. He is the patron saint of Catholic writers and journalists, a declaration made by Pius XI in 1923.
fontes: Saint Francis de Sales, "Introduction to the Devout Life"
Saint Francis de Sales, "Treatise on the Love of God"

itens.resumo: Patriarch of Alexandria in the fifth century, the principal defender of the title Theotokos for Mary at the Council of Ephesus; called the Doctor of the Incarnation.
itens.corpo:
Cyril was born around 376 in Egypt and succeeded his uncle Theophilus as Patriarch of Alexandria in 412. His episcopate was dominated by the controversy against Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who refused to call Mary "Theotokos" (Mother of God), arguing that she had given birth only to the humanity of Christ.

Against Nestorius, Cyril defended the unity of the person of Christ — true God and true man in one person — so that everything affirmed of the incarnate Word, including the maternity of Mary, is affirmed of a single divine subject. His "Letters to Nestorius" and his role at the Council of Ephesus (431), which he presided over as papal legate, led to the condemnation of Nestorianism and the solemn proclamation of the title Theotokos. He also wrote extensive biblical commentaries and treatises on the Trinity.

He died in Alexandria in 444. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1883. Tradition calls him the Doctor of the Incarnation (Doctor Incarnationis) and the "Seal of the Fathers," for the synthesis that his Christology represented for later doctrine, confirmed at the Council of Chalcedon.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: José Luiz — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
fontes: Saint Cyril of Alexandria, "Letters to Nestorius"

itens.resumo: Bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, author of the «Catecheses», a classic instruction on the sacraments of Christian initiation.
itens.corpo:
Cyril was born around 313, probably in the region of Jerusalem, and was ordained bishop of the city around 350. His episcopate was marked by the Trinitarian disputes of the fourth century: because of positions considered ambiguous with regard to Arianism — although he was always, at heart, faithful to the faith of Nicaea —, he was deposed and exiled three times, and was definitively restored after the Council of Constantinople (381), in which he took part.

His main work is the «Catecheses», twenty-four instructions addressed to the catechumens and neophytes of Jerusalem: the first eighteen prepare for baptism, expounding the Creed article by article, and the last five — the «Mystagogical Catecheses» — explain to the newly baptized the meaning of the sacraments they have already received: baptism, chrismation, and the Eucharist. They are one of the most valuable testimonies to the liturgy and catechesis of the ancient Church in Jerusalem.

He died in 386. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1883, together with Cyril of Alexandria. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on March 18.

itens.resumo: Monk and theologian of the eighth century, the last great Father of the Greek Church, defender of sacred images against iconoclasm.
itens.corpo:
John was born around 675 in Damascus, then under Muslim rule, into a Christian family of officials in the administration of the caliphate, a post he also held before retiring to the monastery of Mar Saba, near Jerusalem, where he was ordained a priest.

He wrote the "Fount of Knowledge," a three-part synthesis of philosophy, heresies, and the Christian faith, whose third part, the "Exposition of the Orthodox Faith," is considered the first great systematization of Eastern dogmatic theology and directly influenced later Latin scholasticism. He became the most important theological defender of sacred images during the Byzantine iconoclast crisis, with the "Apologetic Treatises against Those Who Attack the Holy Images," distinguishing between the adoration owed to God alone and the legitimate veneration of images. He also wrote Marian homilies and hymns still used in the Byzantine liturgy.

He died around 749, in the monastery of Mar Saba. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1890. He is considered the last of the great Fathers of the Greek Church, and his work played an important role in the transmission of Eastern patristic theology to the medieval West.
fontes: Saint John of Damascus, "Exposition of the Orthodox Faith"
Saint John of Damascus, "Apologetic Treatises against Those Who Attack the Holy Images"

itens.resumo: English Benedictine monk of the 7th-8th centuries, author of the «Ecclesiastical History of the English People»; called the Doctor of the English.
itens.corpo:
Bede was born around 673 in the kingdom of Northumbria, in England, and at the age of seven was entrusted to the care of the Benedictine monastery of Monkwearmouth-Jarrow, where he lived his whole life as a monk, devoted to study, teaching and writing.

He is the author of the «Ecclesiastical History of the English People» (731), a work that narrates the evangelization of England from the arrival of the Romans to his own time and is considered the most important source for early Anglo-Saxon history. He also wrote biblical commentaries, treatises on chronology — he was one of the first authors to popularize the dating of years "after Christ" (Anno Domini) —, works on the computation of the liturgical calendar, and lives of saints.

He died in Jarrow in 735. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1899, being the first native of Great Britain to receive the title, with the designation Doctor of the English (Doctor Anglorum). His liturgical memorial is celebrated on May 25.
fontes: Leo XIII, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (1899)

itens.resumo: Deacon and poet of the fourth century, the most important Christian author in the Syriac language; called the Doctor of the Syrians.
itens.corpo:
Ephrem was born around 306 in Nisibis, in Roman Mesopotamia, and served there as a deacon and teacher until the city was ceded to Persia in 363, when he took refuge in Edessa, where he continued his teaching ministry until his death.

His work, almost entirely in Syriac verse, comprises hundreds of hymns, among them the cycles "On the Nativity," "On Paradise," "On Faith," and "Against Heresies," as well as biblical commentaries, among them one on the «Diatessaron». His theology, expressed in images and symbols rather than in philosophical categories, became one of the richest sources of the liturgical and spiritual tradition of the Syriac-speaking Churches, and its influence spread, through translations, into Greek and Latin.

He died in Edessa in 373. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XV in 1920, with the title Doctor of the Syrians (Doctor Syrorum). Tradition also calls him the "Harp of the Holy Spirit," for the poetic quality and inspiration of his hymns.

itens.resumo: Sixteenth-century Dutch Jesuit, author of catechisms that shaped Catholic instruction in central Europe during the Counter-Reformation.
itens.corpo:
Peter Canisius was born in 1521 in Nijmegen, in what is now the Netherlands. He entered the newly founded Society of Jesus in 1543, among the first Jesuits, and devoted his life to teaching, preaching and Catholic reform in the German-speaking world, then strongly marked by the spread of Protestantism.

He is the author of three catechisms — the "Great Catechism" (Summa Doctrinae Christianae, 1555), intended for teachers and university students, a medium catechism for secondary school students, and the "Small Catechism" for children —, which went through hundreds of editions and were translated into many languages, becoming one of the main instruments of Catholic formation in central Europe during and after the Council of Trent. He founded Jesuit colleges in Germany, Austria and Switzerland and played a decisive role in halting the advance of Protestantism in those territories.

He died in Fribourg, Switzerland, in 1597. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1925, in the same act in which he was canonized. He is called the "Second Apostle of Germany," in reference to Saint Boniface, because of the importance of his catechetical and missionary work in the region.
fontes: Pius XI, act of canonization and proclamation as Doctor of the Church (May 21, 1925)

itens.resumo: Discalced Carmelite friar of the sixteenth century, co-founder of the Carmelite reform with Saint Teresa of Ávila; called the Mystical Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Juan de Yepes y Álvarez was born in 1542 in Fontiveros, near Ávila. He entered the Carmelite Order in 1563 and, after meeting Teresa of Jesus in 1567, joined her project of reform, becoming, with her, co-founder of the Discalced branch of the Order. Opposition to the reform led to his imprisonment by the Calced Carmelites in Toledo in 1577, where he remained for months in extremely harsh conditions — a period in which he began to compose part of his poetry.

His poetic work and his prose commentaries — the «Dark Night», the «Spiritual Canticle» and the «Ascent of Mount Carmel», among others — describe the path of the soul's purification toward transforming union with God, passing through the "nights" of the senses and of the spirit. Together with Teresa of Ávila, he is considered the greatest exponent of Carmelite mysticism and one of the greatest poets of the Spanish language.

He died in Úbeda in 1591. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1926, with the title of Mystical Doctor. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on December 14.
fontes: Saint John of the Cross, «Dark Night»
Saint John of the Cross, «Spiritual Canticle»
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 2719 (quoting the «Ascent of Mount Carmel»)

itens.resumo: Jesuit cardinal of the 16th-17th centuries, the leading theologian of the Catholic controversy against Protestantism.
itens.corpo:
Robert Bellarmine was born in 1542 in Montepulciano, in Tuscany. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1560 and taught theology at Louvain and at the Roman College, where for years he held the chair of controversial theology, created to respond systematically to Protestant objections.

His main work, the "Disputationes de Controversiis Christianae Fidei," gathers and organizes for the first time in a systematic way the Catholic responses to the Protestant theses on Scripture, the Church, the sacraments, and grace, becoming required reference for both sides of the debate for more than a century. He was created a cardinal in 1599 and appointed Archbishop of Capua; he served as theological consultant in important proceedings of the Roman Curia, among them those involving Giordano Bruno and Galileo Galilei.

He died in Rome in 1621. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1931, the year after his canonization. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on September 17.
fontes: Saint Robert Bellarmine, "Disputationes de Controversiis Christianae Fidei"
Pius XI, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (1931)

itens.resumo: Thirteenth-century Dominican friar, teacher of Thomas Aquinas, notable for his vast philosophical, theological, and scientific work; called the Universal Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Albert was born around 1200 in Lauingen, in Swabia (present-day Germany). He entered the Order of Preachers (Dominicans) around 1223 and taught in several cities of Germany and in Paris, where he had Thomas Aquinas as a disciple, helping to form his intellectual vocation and publicly defending his work after his death, when it was challenged.

His work is of exceptional breadth: he commented on practically the entire known work of Aristotle, which had only recently reached the Latin West by way of the Arabs, and wrote original treatises on botany, zoology, mineralogy, and astronomy, alongside theological works such as the commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard and a «Summa Theologiae». He was one of the first to systematically integrate the method of observing nature into Scholastic theology, which earned him recognition as patron of natural scientists.

He died in Cologne in 1280. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1931, with the title of Universal Doctor (Doctor Universalis), for the encyclopedic breadth of his knowledge. Pius XII declared him patron of those who cultivate the natural sciences in 1941.
fontes: Saint Albert the Great, Commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard

itens.resumo: Portuguese Franciscan friar of the thirteenth century, a celebrated preacher against the heresies of his time; called the Evangelical Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Fernando Martins de Bulhões was born in 1195 in Lisbon. He first entered the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine and, around 1220, impressed by the martyrdom of five Franciscan friars in Morocco, he transferred to the Order of Friars Minor, taking the name Anthony. His talent for preaching was discovered by chance at an ordination in Forlì, and he was sent to preach throughout Italy and southern France, becoming notable for his effectiveness against the heresies of the time, above all Catharism.

At the request of Gregory IX, he wrote the "Sermons for Feast Days" and the "Sunday Sermons," collections that served as models for other preachers, marked by extensive use of allegory and biblical symbolism. He is one of the most popular saints in Catholic devotion, venerated above all as an intercessor for finding lost objects and as patron of the poor, to whom the so-called "Saint Anthony's Bread" is dedicated.

He died near Padua in 1231, at only 35 years of age. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pius XII in 1946, with the title of Evangelical Doctor. According to Benedict XVI, this title reflects how, in his sermons, "the freshness and beauty of the Gospel emerge."
fontes: Saint Anthony of Padua, "Sermons for Feast Days"
Pius XII, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (January 16, 1946)
Benedict XVI, General Audience on Saint Anthony of Padua (February 10, 2010)

itens.resumo: Italian Capuchin friar of the 16th-17th centuries, polyglot preacher and minister general of the Order; called the Apostolic Doctor.
itens.corpo:
Giulio Cesare Russo was born in 1559 in Brindisi, in the Kingdom of Naples. He entered the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin in 1575, taking the name Lawrence, and from his youth stood out for an exceptional gift for languages: besides Italian and Latin, he spoke Hebrew, Greek, German, French and Spanish.

He held positions of great responsibility in the Order, among them that of minister general of the Capuchins, and was employed by the Holy See and by Catholic princes in delicate diplomatic missions, including negotiations to halt the Ottoman advance in central Europe, where he also served as a military chaplain. He left a vast body of written work, gathered in fifteen volumes, notably sermons, the "Mariale" (on the Virgin Mary) and writings of controversy against Lutheranism, such as the "Lutheranismi Hypotyposis".

He died in Lisbon in 1619, during a diplomatic mission. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by John XXIII in 1959, with the title of Apostolic Doctor, because of the intense activity of preaching and mission that characterized his life.
fontes: John XXIII, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (1959)

itens.resumo: A fourteenth-century Dominican tertiary, mystic and adviser to popes, decisive in the return of the papal seat to Rome; co-patroness of Italy and of Europe.
itens.corpo:
Caterina di Jacopo di Benincasa was born in 1347 in Siena, Italy, the twenty-fourth of twenty-five children of a dyer. While still young, she consecrated herself to a life of prayer and penance and, at about the age of eighteen, became a Dominican tertiary, remaining a lay woman and never entering a monastery.

Her reputation for holiness and wisdom led her to correspond with, and to intervene before, the political and ecclesiastical figures of her time, including Pope Gregory XI, whom she urged insistently to return from Avignon to Rome — which in fact took place in 1377, ending the period known as the "Avignon captivity." Her main work, the «Dialogue on Divine Providence», records, in the form of a dialogue between God and a soul, mystical revelations received in ecstasy; she also left numerous letters and prayers.

She died in Rome in 1380, at the age of 33. She was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Paul VI in 1970, a few days after Teresa of Ávila — being the second woman to receive the title. She is co-patroness of Italy, since 1939, and of Europe, since 1999.
fontes: Saint Catherine of Siena, «Dialogue on Divine Providence»
Paul VI, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (October 4, 1970)
John Paul II, Apostolic Letter «Spes Aedificandi» (1999)

itens.titulo: Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus
itens.resumo: French Discalced Carmelite of the nineteenth century, author of «Story of a Soul» and of the spiritual doctrine of the "little way"; the youngest Doctor of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Marie Françoise-Thérèse Martin was born in 1873 in Alençon, in Normandy. She entered the Carmel of Lisieux while still a teenager, at the age of fifteen, with a special dispensation obtained personally from Pope Leo XIII, and lived there as a contemplative religious until her death at the age of 24, a victim of tuberculosis.

Out of obedience to her superiors, she wrote her memoirs, published posthumously as «Story of a Soul», in which she sets forth the "little way" of spiritual childhood: attaining holiness not through great deeds, but through total trust in God and through love lived in the small, ordinary things of daily life. The work enjoyed enormous popular circulation and spiritual influence throughout the twentieth century.

She died in Lisieux in 1897. She was canonized in 1925 and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by John Paul II in 1997, by the Apostolic Letter «Divini Amoris Scientia» ("The Science of Divine Love") — being the youngest and one of the few women, until then, to receive the title. She is co-patroness of the missions, alongside Saint Francis Xavier.
fontes: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, «Story of a Soul»
John Paul II, Apostolic Letter «Divini Amoris Scientia» (October 19, 1997)

itens.resumo: Spanish priest and preacher of the sixteenth century, teacher of important saints of the Catholic reform; called the Apostle of Andalusia.
itens.corpo:
John of Ávila was born in 1499 in Almodóvar del Campo, in the region of Toledo. He studied law and then theology and philosophy at Alcalá de Henares, and was ordained a priest with the intention of going as a missionary to the Indies; at the request of the Archbishop of Seville, however, he remained in Spain, devoting himself to the evangelization of Andalusia.

His preaching and spiritual direction directly influenced central figures of the Spanish Catholic reform of the sixteenth century, among them Ignatius of Loyola, Teresa of Ávila, John of God, Francis Borgia and Luis of Granada. His most important written work, the «Audi, Filia» ("Listen, daughter"), a treatise on spiritual direction begun at the request of a young penitent, sets out an itinerary of Christian life founded on prayer and self-knowledge.

He died in Montilla, in Andalusia, in 1569. He was canonized in 2012 and, in the same year, proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI, during the Synod of Bishops on the New Evangelization. He is called the "Apostle of Andalusia".
fontes: Benedict XVI, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (October 7, 2012)

itens.resumo: German Benedictine abbess of the twelfth century, mystic, composer, and naturalist; one of the few women Doctors of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Hildegard was born around 1098 in Bermersheim, on the Rhine, and from childhood was entrusted to the religious life, entering the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg. She became abbess in 1136 and later founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg, near Bingen.

From childhood she had visions which, from the age of forty, with ecclesiastical authorization, she began to record in writing: the «Scivias» ("Know the Ways"), the «Liber Vitae Meritorum» and the «Liber Divinorum Operum» form a visionary theological trilogy of great originality. She was also a composer — she left an extensive body of liturgical chants and the «Ordo Virtutum», considered one of the first examples of liturgical drama — and she wrote treatises on medicine and natural history, in addition to maintaining correspondence with popes, bishops, and emperors.

She died in 1179. She was canonized by equivalent means and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XVI in 2012. She is one of the few women, to this day, to receive the title of Doctor of the Church.
fontes: Saint Hildegard of Bingen, «Liber Divinorum Operum»
Benedict XVI, proclamation as Doctor of the Church (October 7, 2012)

itens.resumo: Armenian monk and poet of the 10th-11th centuries, author of the "Book of Lamentations"; the first Doctor of the Church from the Armenian tradition.
itens.corpo:
Gregory of Narek (Grigor Narekatsi) was born around 951, in a village on the shores of Lake Van, in historical Armenia (present-day eastern Turkey). He lived as a monk in the monastery of Narek, where he devoted himself to the study of Scripture, theology and poetry.

His masterpiece, the "Book of Lamentations" (or "Narek"), completed around 1002, comprises 95 chapters and more than ten thousand verses in the form of a personal, penitential prayer addressed to God — one of the greatest monuments of Armenian spiritual literature, still used devotionally today by the faithful of the Armenian Apostolic Church, who have venerated him as a saint for centuries.

He died around 1003-1010. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pope Francis in 2015, becoming the first saint of the Armenian tradition to receive the title — a recognition that also reflects the Catholic Church's esteem for the Armenian Apostolic Church, with which it is not in full communion. The proclamation was announced on the occasion of the centenary of the Armenian genocide.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Hovhannes Asatryan SutiComposer — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
fontes: Saint Gregory of Narek, "Book of Lamentations"
Francis, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (April 12, 2015)

itens.resumo: Bishop of Lyon in the 2nd-3rd centuries, the most important anti-Gnostic theologian of the early Church; called the Doctor of Unity.
itens.corpo:
Irenaeus was probably born around 130-140 in Smyrna, in Asia Minor, where in his youth he heard the preaching of Polycarp, a disciple, according to tradition, of the Apostle John himself — which makes Irenaeus a link between the apostolic generation and the Church of the 2nd century. He later settled in Lyon, in Gaul, where he became a presbyter and, around 177-178, succeeded Pothinus, who had died during a persecution, as bishop.

His main work, «Against Heresies» («Adversus Haereses»), in five books, is the most complete refutation of Gnosticism produced by the ancient Church: it sets out and refutes in detail the Gnostic systems, especially that of Valentinus, and formulates, in response, a theology of apostolic tradition, of the unity of the Scriptures, and of the recapitulation of all creation in Christ. He is considered by many historians to be the founder of Christian systematic theology.

He died in the early 3rd century, probably in Lyon — later tradition, without historical certainty, attributes his death to martyrdom. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Pope Francis in 2022, with the title Doctor of Unity (Doctor Unitatis), both for the doctrinal unity he defended against Gnosticism and for the bond between East and West that his figure represents.
fontes: Francis, act of proclamation as Doctor of the Church (January 21, 2022)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 79 (quotation from Saint Irenaeus)

itens.resumo: Pope from 440 to 461, author of the «Tome to Flavian» on the two natures of Christ, decisive at the Council of Chalcedon.
itens.corpo:
Leo was born around 400, probably in Tuscany. Before being elected Bishop of Rome in 440, he already held prominent positions in the papal administration as a deacon, having been sent on a diplomatic mission to Gaul by the Emperor Valentinian III.

His pontificate faced two great crises: the doctrinal one, with the controversy over the nature of Christ stirred up by Eutyches, and the political one, with the barbarian invasions of Italy. On the first, he wrote the «Tome to Flavian» (449), an exposition of the faith in Christ as one person in two natures, divine and human, "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation" — a formula that, acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon (451) with the words "Peter has spoken through Leo", became the classic Christological definition of Catholic orthodoxy. On the second, he is remembered for having gone, in 452, to meet Attila, king of the Huns, and persuading him not to advance on Rome.

He died in Rome in 461. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XIV in 1754. He is, with Gregory the Great and Nicholas I, one of the few popes to whom tradition grants the title "Great." His liturgical memorial is celebrated on November 10.
fontes: Saint Leo the Great, «Tome to Flavian»

itens.resumo: English cardinal and convert from Anglicanism, proclaimed in 2025 the 38th and most recent Doctor of the Church.
itens.corpo:
John Henry Newman (1801-1890) was the leading theologian of the Oxford Movement before converting to Catholicism in 1845. As a Catholic, he developed an original reflection on the historical development of Christian doctrine, on the nature of faith and moral conscience, and on the role of the laity in the life of the Church, expressed above all in works such as the "Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine" (1845) and the "Grammar of Assent" (1870).

Created a cardinal in 1879 by Pope Leo XIII without ever having been consecrated a bishop, Newman was beatified by Benedict XVI in 2010 and canonized by Pope Francis on October 13, 2019. His influence left a particular mark on the ecclesiology and the theology of conscience taken up by the Second Vatican Council.

On November 1, 2025, the Solemnity of All Saints, Pope Leo XIV proclaimed him the 38th Doctor of the Universal Church — the first to receive this title since the proclamation of Saint Gregory of Narek in 2015, and the first English-speaking saint to receive it —, also declaring him co-patron, alongside Saint Thomas Aquinas, of all who take part in the educational process.
fontes: Leo XIV, homily for the proclamation as Doctor of the Church (November 1, 2025)
